ReactorSockets.CloseReason.html.summary: Enum CloseReason Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Why a Link closed, defined and kept stable by this library rather than borrowed from a platform enumeration (ADR 0008): a consumer's permanent logic switches on this instead of a SocketError that differs between Windows and Unix. The exact SocketError travels in the DiagnosticRecord emitted at the same moment, linked to this only by the Link and the Pump it happened in. public enum CloseReason Fields LocalClose = 0 The consumer called Close on this Link. ResetByRemote = 1 The remote end reset the connection. Named for the remote rather than a "peer" deliberately: Peer is a Session word, and Raw leaves it free for whatever a consumer's own protocol layer calls its remote party. This is the same "remote" RemoteOf(LinkId) answers for. Refused = 2 The remote end refused the connection. Unreachable = 3 The destination was reported unreachable. Failed = 4 The Link failed for a reason not covered by the other members.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.En.title: Property Endpoints | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.En.summary: Property Endpoints Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Endpoints The endpoints to bind at construction, in the order supplied; possibly empty. Declared once and never rebound (ADR 0014) — a Session's addresses are part of what it is, not something it acquires later. An empty set binds nothing until the first dial, which binds a single wildcard, port-zero socket in the destination's address family. Provenance: empty is the absence of a declaration, not a chosen address — the dial-only socket's family and port are derived from the destination and the OS, never configured. public IReadOnlyList<IPEndPoint> Endpoints { get; init; } Property Value IReadOnlyList<IPEndPoint>

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.En.title: Property Entropy | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.En.summary: Property Entropy Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Entropy The entropy the cookie secrets, session ids and resume secrets are drawn from. A construction knob in ADR 0012's sense — the consumer's own resource, and a consumer with a hardware source or a policy about which generator may be used is entitled to supply it. It carries a default only because that default is derived rather than guessed. Provenance: the platform's own CSPRNG. public RandomNumberGenerator Entropy { get; init; } Property Value RandomNumberGenerator Remarks Nothing disposes this, and nothing should. A supplied generator belongs to the consumer, who may hand the same one to several Reactors; a Reactor that disposed it would be disposing a resource it does not own. The default instance is not a leak either — on .NET the generator Create() returns holds no handle, drawing from the OS on each call, so its Dispose has nothing to release.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Fr.title: Property FragmentSize | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Fr.summary: Property FragmentSize Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll FragmentSize The bytes a fragment carries, and therefore the unit every buffer here is measured in. Defaults to 1200. Provenance: QUIC's floor beneath the 1280-byte IPv6 minimum MTU (RFC 9000), the one value with citable provenance for surviving an arbitrary path. Must lie between 576 (RFC 791's guaranteed reassembly minimum) and 65 507 (the maximum UDP payload). public int? FragmentSize { get; init; } Property Value int? Remarks Announced in the handshake (ADR 0024). Each Peer cuts its reliable Messages at the smaller of this value and the peer's announced value, fixed once when the Peer reaches Established and unchanged across a Resume, so two Reactors configured with different values interoperate. A reliable Fragment wider than this value closes the Peer with ProtocolViolation, which only a non-conforming peer causes. The same smaller value is the single-Datagram cap of an unreliable Message, refused above it with MessageTooLarge. A later change to this options instance never reaches a Peer already open. See ResolvedFragmentSize.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.He.title: Property HeldRecordBudgetBytes | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.He.summary: Property HeldRecordBudgetBytes Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll HeldRecordBudgetBytes The most heap, in bytes, a Reactor's ReliableOrdered Spaces can hold in ordinary records waiting behind a gap, across all its Peers: Capacity × 2 × ReceiveWindowFragments × FragmentSize, with each slot's bookkeeping. public long HeldRecordBudgetBytes { get; } Property Value long Remarks This is a ceiling reached only under traffic, not a line allocated at construction, so ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.ValidateMemoryBill() does not count it. It is over and above ReceiveBudgetBytes and about the same size. A record past either limit is left unacknowledged and counted on OutOfWindowPackets, so the far end's retransmission brings it back when the Space has moved. The figure counts what stays held, not the short-lived arrays the ring leaves behind each time it grows.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Li.title: Property Linger | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Li.summary: Property Linger Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Linger How long a closing Session stays alive to retransmit its Goodbye and absorb what is still in flight. Required, for the same reason as SendIdleInterval: it trades a prompt teardown against a clean one. At most 2^32 - 1 milliseconds (about 49.7 days), the most a handshake may announce. public required TimeSpan Linger { get; init; } Property Value TimeSpan

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Ma.title: Property MaxDatagramsPerPump | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Ma.summary: Property MaxDatagramsPerPump Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll MaxDatagramsPerPump The most reads one Pump makes on each bound socket, so a flood cannot keep a Pump from returning. Defaults to ResolvedMaxDatagramsPerPump. Provenance: derived from a full Reactor's worth of traffic, as AdmissionCap is (ADR 0012). At least 1. public int? MaxDatagramsPerPump { get; init; } Property Value int? Remarks What this leaves unread waits in the socket's receive buffer for a later Pump. If that buffer fills, the operating system drops what arrives next and no counter here sees it. A queued socket error spends a read too. Reads are first come, first served, so a live Peer's datagrams wait behind a flood from anyone else on that socket, and a long enough wait looks to the receive-idle deadline like silence. Lower this to bound how long one Pump can take, at the cost of a longer wait. A Pump that reaches it reports DatagramReadLimitReached.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Ma.title: Property MaxMessageSize | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Ma.summary: Property MaxMessageSize Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll MaxMessageSize The largest Message, in bytes, this Reactor will accept or deliver. Required: it is a statement about the consumer's own protocol that nothing here can derive. It is also the knob that multiplies this profile's memory bill in more than one direction — the class remarks on DatagramSessionOptions say what it floors and what raising it costs. public required int MaxMessageSize { get; init; } Property Value int Remarks Announced to the peer at the handshake precisely so an oversized claim can be refused before this end holds anything for it: a declared Fragment fragmentCount larger than this Reactor's receive window (ResolvedReceiveWindowFragments) is closed on its first Fragment, before any receive-window slot or Fragment-group bookkeeping exists for it. The bound is the window rather than ReceiveWindowFloor alone, because the floor is computed from this end's own ResolvedFragmentSize: a conforming peer with a smaller fragment size legally cuts the same, within-limit Message into more Fragments than the floor, up to the announced window (ADR 0024). ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Validate() already requires the window to be at least the floor, so a set at exactly this value is always admitted.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Ma.title: Property MaxPeersPerAddress | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Ma.summary: Property MaxPeersPerAddress Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll MaxPeersPerAddress The most accepted Peers one address may hold at once, so one reachable address cannot occupy every capacity Slot. Defaults to ResolvedMaxPeersPerAddress, one fewer than Capacity. Provenance: derived from capacity, as the largest limit that still keeps one address from holding every Slot (ADR 0014). How many Peers legitimately share an address depends on the NATs and proxies in front of this Reactor, so set it lower when strangers can reach it. At least 1. A value of Capacity or above sets no limit, which is what the default is at a capacity of 1. public int? MaxPeersPerAddress { get; init; } Property Value int? Remarks The count is by address, without the port: a host can answer a Cookie from as many ports as it can bind, so a limit that counted ports would limit nothing. The address family and IPv6 scope stay in the key, because they distinguish hosts (ADR 0014). IPv6 addresses are counted by the prefix PeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength sets, so a host that can bind a whole prefix gets the limit once. IPv4 addresses are counted whole. A Peer is charged to the address its handshake came from for as long as it holds its Slot, including while Interrupted or Closing and after a Resume moves it to another address. A dialled Peer is not charged: this Reactor chose to make it. A handshake over the limit is refused the same way as one at a full Reactor, and reported with AddressPeerLimitReached.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Mi.title: Property MissedHeartbeats | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Mi.summary: Property MissedHeartbeats Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll MissedHeartbeats How many consecutive heartbeat intervals may pass in silence before a Peer is declared gone. Defaults to 3. Provenance: RFC 4271's hold time, three times the keepalive interval. Must be at least 2, because a count of 1 makes a single lost datagram fatal and no network is that reliable. public int? MissedHeartbeats { get; init; } Property Value int?

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Pe.title: Property PeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Pe.summary: Property PeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll PeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength How many leading bits of an IPv6 address form the key for MaxPeersPerAddress, so every address in one prefix shares one limit. Defaults to ResolvedPeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength, 64. Provenance: RFC 4291 §2.5.1 fixes the interface identifier of a unicast address at 64 bits, so a /64 is one link (ADR 0014). From 1 to 128. A value of 128 counts each address on its own. public int? PeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength { get; init; } Property Value int? Remarks Every on-link host on an IPv6 LAN shares one /64, so at the default those Peers share one limit. Set 128 when Peers legitimately arrive from one link. A shorter length groups more of a customer's delegated prefix, at the cost of grouping unrelated customers. The scope stays in the key, so link-local addresses are grouped per interface. IPv4 addresses are never grouped.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.title: Property ReceiveBudgetBytes | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.summary: Property ReceiveBudgetBytes Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll ReceiveBudgetBytes The receive line of the memory bill in bytes, as a long so that a combination too large to allocate is a value this can report rather than an overflow it silently wraps through. public long ReceiveBudgetBytes { get; } Property Value long Remarks Four things per Peer scale with the window, and this figure covers all four. Payload slots — ResolvedFragmentSize bytes each — exist only for the ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.ReliableSpaceCount Spaces that hold fragments until a Message is whole. The one-byte-per-slot admission record a receive window classifies against exists for all ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.SpaceCount Spaces, because all four classify whether or not they retain. ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.FragmentLengthBytes per slot records how many bytes of a held Fragment's payload are actually occupied, and ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.FragmentGroupEntryBytes per slot names the group that payload belongs to — both exist only for the same ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.ReliableSpaceCount Spaces as the payload they describe, and both are the receive window's own reassembly bookkeeping, not a separate buffer: the length says a piece was held, the group-identity entry is what still lets an abandoned set's held and declared counts be read once that slot is reused. The six-byte waiting-group entry — ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.PendingGroupEntryBytes — exists for the same two Spaces too, but only half a window's worth each (ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.PendingGroupsPerSpace), since a completed-but-undelivered group holds at least two Fragments. This figure is an exact statement of what the receive arena takes at construction. Ordinary records held behind a gap are the one receive-side cost outside it, and they have their own ceiling, HeldRecordBudgetBytes.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.title: Property ReceiveWindowFloor | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.summary: Property ReceiveWindowFloor Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll ReceiveWindowFloor The resolved receive window: ReceiveWindowFragments if set, otherwise the fragments one maximum Message occupies. public int ReceiveWindowFloor { get; } Property Value int

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.title: Property ReceiveWindowFragments | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.summary: Property ReceiveWindowFragments Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll ReceiveWindowFragments The fragments each reliable Space may have outstanding per Peer. Defaults to exactly the number a maximum Message occupies. Provenance: derived from MaxMessageSize and FragmentSize — ADR 0004's deadlock floor rather than a performance choice: a window narrower than one whole Message can never deliver one, so it can never advance, so the sender can never send the rest. This resolved value is also the inbound bound a declared Fragment fragmentCount is checked against: a set larger than the window can never be reassembled, since there is no slot to hold every one of its pieces at once, so DatagramSessionReactor closes it before any is held. public int? ReceiveWindowFragments { get; init; } Property Value int?

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.title: Property ResolvedFragmentSize | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.summary: Property ResolvedFragmentSize Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll ResolvedFragmentSize The resolved fragment size: FragmentSize if set, otherwise 1200. public int ResolvedFragmentSize { get; } Property Value int Remarks This is the value the handshake announces. A Peer fixes its send Fragment size once, when it reaches Established, at the smaller of this value and the peer's announced value (ADR 0024). Every Send(PeerId, DeliveryMode, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) call for that Peer, and every retransmit, cuts by that fixed value rather than reading this property afresh, so fragment size cannot move mid-Session even if this options instance later would resolve differently.

ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.title: Property RetentionSlots | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Re.summary: Property RetentionSlots Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll RetentionSlots The uniform retention slots one reliable Space holds per Peer: RetentionBytes divided by ResolvedFragmentSize, truncating any remainder. Stays derived from the byte bound rather than a knob of its own (ADR 0012) so it cannot drift from RetentionBytes when the fragment size changes. ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Se.title: Property SendIdleInterval | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionOptions.Se.summary: Property SendIdleInterval Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll SendIdleInterval How long a Session may go without sending before it sends a Ping instead. Required: shorter costs bandwidth on an idle link, longer costs time to notice a dead Peer, and only the consumer knows which they would rather spend. There is no option to disable this: every Established Peer that has sent no data datagram for this long is always sent one seven-byte control record, whatever else it did or did not receive. At most 2^32 - 1 milliseconds (about 49.7 days), the most a handshake may announce. public required TimeSpan SendIdleInterval { get; init; } Property Value TimeSpan Remarks The Ping this produces is a Heartbeat, and a Heartbeat is not a keepalive: it proves the party behind this Session is still there — able to receive and eventually acknowledge application data — not merely that some NAT mapping between here and there is still open, which a bare keepalive a middlebox itself could answer would not prove. The receive side is derived, not configured: a Peer is declared gone after the remote's announced interval times MissedHeartbeats of silence (ADR 0012).

Guessing any of them would be guessing at the consumer's application. Values fixed by the wire format are not here at all and cannot be reached from here: the 32-bit acknowledgement width, the 64-entry duplicate window, the four sequence Spaces, zero as the reserved session id, the 20-byte data header and the thirty-second cookie epoch are protocol constants. Changing one changes what a datagram means, which is a version, not a setting. The memory bill. A Reactor built from these options preallocates, and the whole of it is these two lines: receive: Capacity × 2 × ReceiveWindowFragments × FragmentSize — two of the four Spaces are reliable and reassemble, and each holds a window of whole fragment slots per Peer. send: Capacity × 2 × RetentionBytes — the same two Spaces retain what they have sent until it is acknowledged, per Peer. FragmentSize is in one line and not the other because the window counts packets and retention counts bytes. Neither line has a traffic term: both are allocated at construction and never grow. Each line also carries a few bytes of bookkeeping per fragment slot, which ReceiveBudgetBytes and SendBudgetBytes include exactly — under 2% at the default fragment size. The frame arena (ArenaSize) is over and above those two lines and is shared across the whole Reactor rather than multiplied by capacity. One further cost is allocated only under traffic: ordinary ReliableOrdered records waiting behind a gap. It has a ceiling of its own, HeldRecordBudgetBytes, and reaching it refuses further records rather than growing. MaxMessageSize reaches three places at once: it is announced to the remote as a receive limit, it floors the receive window at the fragments one maximum Message occupies (ReceiveWindowFloor), and it floors the frame arena, because an arena that cannot hold one maximum Message could never deliver one. The limit is enforced as well as announced: a completed Message above it is discarded rather than delivered, with OversizedMessage. Careless enlargement grows memory in two directions rather than one: the window floor is per Peer, so the receive line above rises with it multiplied by capacity and by the Spaces, and the shared arena is pushed up alongside. Retention is the exception this profile makes. RetentionBytes is floored by ResolvedFragmentSize rather than by MaxMessageSize, because a reliable Space retransmits fragment by fragment and needs only one fragment to have something to resend. Security. The session field on every datagram is a demultiplexing token, not an authenticator: it makes blind off-path injection a 32-bit guess, and does nothing against anyone who has seen one datagram of the Session. This library does not encrypt, and on-path attackers are out of scope (ADR 0009). A consumer who needs confidentiality or integrity against an on-path attacker provides it themselves, inside the Message. A Message too wide for its mode to carry is refused before any work is done on it: no sequence is allocated and no retention is taken, so a rejected Send leaves no trace on the Session. How wide is too wide depends on the mode and is decided by Resolve(int, int, DeliveryMode, uint, int), the one place the rule is stated: an unreliable mode is capped at a single Datagram and refused above it as MessageTooLarge, a reliable mode fragments, and every mode is refused above a second cap as RemoteMessageTooLarge (ADR 0004). That second cap is peer's own announced receive limit, captured on its Slot at handshake, not this Reactor's own MaxMessageSize: Send is therefore not purely local to this Reactor's configuration, because the same payload can be accepted for one Peer and refused for another whose handshake announced a smaller limit. That gate sits behind the peer lookup rather than in front of it, because both caps it measures against, fragment size and remote max message size alike, are the Peer's own captured values; a Peer this Reactor is not holding open returns Closed whatever the Message's width. Past that gate, a reliable mode allocates the next sequence in its own Space and retains the Message whole there, returning RetentionExhausted once that Space has no slot left — and that refusal spends nothing either: the sequence is claimed only once retention has committed, so a refused reliable Send leaves the Space's next sequence exactly where it was, rather than opening a gap the receiver's window would wait on for a record that is never sent; Unreliable and UnreliableSequenced still allocate a sequence — every mode gets one, the same as every other (ReactorSockets.Session.OutboundSequenceSpaces) — but retain nothing, because nothing unreliable is ever retransmitted. A Message this call accepts is queued on peer's Slot (ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionReactor.PeerSlot.PendingSends) and leaves as one packet record inside the next Pump()'s single coalesced Datagram to that Peer, in Send order (ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionReactor.FlushOutboundDatagrams()) — nothing reaches the wire before that Pump runs, and a Send with no following Pump puts nothing on the wire at all. The bytes are copied before this call returns — into ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionReactor._retention for a reliable mode, into the queued record for an unreliable one — so the caller owns its buffer again the instant Send returns and may overwrite or reuse it without changing what is eventually put on the wire. A Message wider than this Peer's send Fragment size (fragmentSize below: the smaller of this Reactor's ResolvedFragmentSize and the peer's announced Fragment size) cannot fit in one Datagram, and for Unreliable and UnreliableSequenced that cap is reported back as MessageTooLarge rather than thrown, and it is permanent — no option lifts it: you may only fragment what you can retransmit (ADR 0004), because fragmenting what cannot be repaired multiplies the failure rate by the number of pieces — a ten-Fragment unreliable Message on a path losing 1% of Datagrams arrives about 90% of the time, having spent ten Datagrams of bandwidth on a coin flip (docs/delivery-modes.md). A Message within that cap but wider than peer's own announced MaxMessageSize is refused with RemoteMessageTooLarge, because the far end would discard it on arrival; a Message over both caps reports MessageTooLarge. For ReliableOrdered and ReliableUnordered the single-Datagram cap does not apply: a Message up to peer's own announced MaxMessageSize (see the summary above) is cut into ceil(length / fragmentSize) Fragments, each retained and sequenced as its own ordinary reliable packet, and a Message wider than that remote limit is refused with RemoteMessageTooLarge. That fragmentSize is this Peer's ReactorSockets.DatagramSessionReactor.PeerSlot.FragmentSize: the smaller of this Reactor's ResolvedFragmentSize and the Fragment size the peer announced, fixed once when the Peer reached Established (ADR 0024) — not re-read on this or any later call, and unchanged by a Resume. A retransmit re-sends bytes already cut, so two Messages sent to the same Peer at different times, and every retransmit of either, are cut with the same size. A reliable Message that needs more Fragments at that size than the peer's announced receive window holds is refused with RemoteMessageTooLarge, with nothing retained or sequenced. Returns SendOutcome Remarks RetentionExhausted is reachable from one Send call (ADR 0004's "one Message can fill the send window alone"): the retention budget is sized in Fragments, not Messages, so a single Message cut into more Fragments than its Space has free slots for exhausts that Space by itself, with nothing else needing to have sent anything first. A half-retained Message would be unrepairable: the receiver's reassembly waits forever for a set that was never cut in full. A smaller Message that fits the Space's free slots still succeeds afterward — the refusal costs the Space nothing. Sending to a peer this Reactor is not currently holding open — unknown, or already closed — returns Closed rather than throwing, unlike CountersOf(PeerId): a Peer closing under a caller is an ordinary race, the same reason Close(PeerId) tolerates a stale PeerId. ReactorSockets.DeliveryMode.html.summary: Enum DeliveryMode Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Which of a datagram Session's four delivery modes carries a Message sent through Send(PeerId, DeliveryMode, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) (ADR 0009). See docs/delivery-modes.md for the consumer-facing guide to choosing one and the full guarantees each mode makes: ordering, duplicate suppression, and what a late arrival does. Each mode is carried in its own Space. public enum DeliveryMode Fields Unreliable = 0 Delivered at most once per send, in whatever order it arrives, deduplicated within a bounded sliding window. Nothing under this mode is ever retransmitted. UnreliableSequenced = 1 Delivered only if it is strictly newer than the last Message this mode delivered; a Message superseded before it arrives is discarded rather than delivered late. Nothing under this mode is ever retransmitted. ReliableUnordered = 2 Always delivered, in whatever order it arrives. Retransmitted until acknowledged, retaining what was sent in this mode's own reliable Space. ReliableOrdered = 3 Always delivered, in the order it was sent — a Message held up in transit blocks every later Message in this mode's Space until it arrives. Retransmitted until acknowledged, retaining what was sent in this mode's own reliable Space. Remarks Explicit values throughout, the same house style as DisconnectReason and SendOutcome: a member is added at the end with the next free number, never inserted, so a value a consumer has already persisted keeps its meaning across a library upgrade. ReactorSockets.DiagnosticId.html.summary: Enum DiagnosticId Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll A closed, permanent enumeration of diagnostic causes with explicit values in reserved blocks — common 1-99, Raw 100-199, datagram session 200-299, stream session 300-399 (ADR 0013) — so a future insertion cannot silently renumber an id a consumer has persisted. There is no None or Unknown member and zero is never used: every DiagnosticRecord has a cause by construction. public enum DiagnosticId Fields AdmissionCapReached = 1 The configured admission cap was hit this Pump with work still waiting to be admitted. No subject. Value0 is the cap, Value1 is the count of Admissions declined, counted as the Reactor's counters count them: once per declining where the work waits out of reach — a listening Link or bound endpoint with a pending connection it left in the OS backlog, never the number of connections left there, a depth unknowable without accepting — and once per piece of work where the Reactor was holding it, whether it then waits or is Discarded. ArenaExhausted = 2 The frame arena had no room left for a request, regardless of the read-share escape. Subject is the Link that made the request on Raw, and the Peer whose Message could not be reserved on either session profile (ADR 0014). Value0 is the bytes requested, Value1 is the arena's bytes free at the moment of the request. CapacityExhausted = 3 Every capacity slot was occupied this Pump with work still waiting to be admitted — a different exhaustion from AdmissionCapReached, reachable because the admission cap can be configured above Capacity. No subject. Value0 is the capacity, Value1 is the count of Admissions declined, counted the same way and with the same limit as AdmissionCapReached's. LinkFailed = 100 A registered Link failed and closed. Subject is the Link. Value0 carries the platform SocketError as its underlying integer value; Value1 is unused. DestinationUnreachable = 101 An ICMP port-unreachable (or platform equivalent) was reported for a send. Subject is the Link. Value0 carries the platform SocketError as its underlying integer value; Value1 is unused. DatagramTruncated = 102 A datagram exceeded the Reactor's scratch buffer and was truncated. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the scratch buffer size in bytes; Value1 is unused. DatagramMalformed = 200 A datagram was discarded because nothing in it could be attributed to a Peer: wrong length, an unknown control type, a body the declared type cannot fill, padding that was not zero, a session id naming no Session, or a well-formed control reply — a Cookie, an Accept, a Refusal — matching no dial this Reactor is waiting on. That last case is not a parse failure, but it is the same thing to a consumer: bytes arrived, named nobody, and went nowhere. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the bytes received; Value1 is unused. A remote can produce this at will by sending rubbish, which is exactly why it is a Diagnostic and never an Event: the event stream is the consumer's protocol, and an unauthenticated stranger must not be able to write to it. Warn rather than Error for the same reason — nothing is wrong with this Reactor. CookieRejected = 201 A Hello carried a cookie this Reactor did not mint, or minted too long ago: a forged or corrupted authenticator, a cookie replayed from a different source address, or one from an epoch older than the previous. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the epoch the cookie offered; Value1 is the epoch current at the moment it was checked. Warn, never Error: a cookie arriving one epoch after it was minted is the mechanism working, and a Reactor visible to the internet will see forged ones continuously. Raising this to Error would train a consumer to ignore Error. VersionRefused = 202 A cookie-validated Hello offered a protocol version this Reactor does not speak, and was refused. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the version offered; Value1 is the version this Reactor requires. Emitted only for a Hello that passed the cookie check, because that is the only Hello a Reactor answers at all — a bare Hello is answered with a Cookie and nothing else, whatever version it claimed. FragmentSetAbandoned = 203 A Fragment set for an established Peer was abandoned before it ever completed. Subject is the Peer, not the claimed Source: an incomplete set belongs to the Session that was receiving it, not to a bare source address. Value0 is the number of fragments actually held for the set at the moment it was abandoned; Value1 is the number the set's own metadata declared it would need. Held against expected is the pair a consumer can act on — one of forty held is a path dropping almost everything of that size, thirty-nine of forty is ordinary loss on a set that was nearly there, and the two want different responses. Warn, not Error: nothing local is broken, an abandoned set is loss on a lossy transport working as designed, and the level's job is to answer whether a consumer wants to see this, not whether this Reactor is at fault. RetransmissionTimerBackedOff = 204 This Peer's ReactorSockets.RetransmissionTimer backed off: a Pump's expiry sweep (ReactorSockets.Session.OutstandingReliableSequences.CollectExpired(ReactorSockets.Session.PacketRecordMode)) found at least one overdue sequence on either reliable Space, so ReactorSockets.RetransmissionTimer.BackOff() was called once for the Peer and every sequence the sweep reported re-armed at the single resulting RTO. Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the new RTO in milliseconds — EffectiveTimeout(TimeSpan, TimeSpan) at the moment of the backoff; Value1 is ReactorSockets.RetransmissionTimer.ConsecutiveBackoffs after this backoff. Trace, not Warn: this is protocol machinery working correctly, not a fault. A lossy path emits it continuously — every Pump that finds an overdue sequence backs off again — and raising it above Trace would train a consumer to ignore the level it sits at. OversizedFragmentSet = 205 An established Peer's Fragment declared a fragmentCount larger than this Reactor's own receive window could ever hold, and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation on that Fragment's first appearance, before any receive-window slot or Fragment-group bookkeeping was created for its set. Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the declared fragmentCount; Value1 is the largest legal count this Reactor's ResolvedReceiveWindowFragments allows. Warn, for the same reason as DatagramMalformed: a remote can produce this at will by lying about how many Fragments a Message needs. UnreliableFragment = 206 A packet record carried the fragment shape in one of the two unreliable modes, which ADR 0004 forbids — you may only fragment what you can retransmit — and the read failed outright, taking the whole Datagram with it. Subject is the claimed Source, not the Peer, matching the DatagramMalformed that is raised alongside it: a discarded Datagram is never attributed to the Session it named, and no byte of it is counted against that Peer. Value0 is the mode the record claimed, as the two mode bits' wire value — 0 for Unreliable, 1 for UnreliableSequenced; Value1 is unused. Warn, for the same reason as DatagramMalformed: a remote can produce this at will, and nothing is wrong with this Reactor. Distinct from DatagramMalformed rather than folded into it because the two say different things to a consumer. A malformed Datagram is rubbish from anywhere; this one is well-formed at every level but the rule, which means the sender is running a build that fragments in modes this profile does not — a misconfiguration a consumer can act on, and the send path already refuses to produce. OversizedMessage = 207 A completed Message, whole or reassembled from its Fragments, was larger than this Reactor's own MaxMessageSize and was discarded instead of delivered. Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the Message's length in bytes; Value1 is this Reactor's MaxMessageSize. The Session stays open, and a discarded reliable Message stays acknowledged, so the far end does not resend it and later Messages are unaffected. Warn, for the same reason as DatagramMalformed: a remote can produce this at will, and nothing is wrong with this Reactor. AddressPeerLimitReached = 208 A verified handshake, or on the stream profile an accepted connection, was refused because its address already holds MaxPeersPerAddress or MaxPeersPerAddress accepted Peers while other capacity Slots were free. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the limit; Value1 is the prefix length the address was counted by: 32 for IPv4, and PeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength or PeerLimitIPv6PrefixLength for IPv6, so every address in that prefix shares the limit. One record per refusal, because it names the address and the admission cap already bounds how many refusals a Pump can make. A full Reactor reports CapacityExhausted on the datagram profile and PeerRefused on the stream profile instead. Warn: a remote can produce this at will, and a consumer can act on it by raising the limit if the address is a NAT or proxy, or by blocking it if it is not. Defined by the datagram profile and shared by the stream profile, because it is one condition (ADR 0020). DatagramReadLimitReached = 209 A Pump made MaxDatagramsPerPump reads on one bound socket and stopped. What was left, if anything, waits for a later Pump. No subject. Value0 is the limit; Value1 is the socket's index in BoundEndpoints. At most one record per bound socket per Pump. Warn: a remote can produce this at will, and it names a configured bound a consumer can act on. A queued socket error spends a read, so not every read was a datagram. The socket's queue depth cannot be read past queued errors, so a Pump that read exactly the last queued datagram also reports this. OversizedFragment = 210 An established Peer's reliable Fragment carried more payload bytes than this Reactor's own ResolvedFragmentSize, and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation before anything in that Datagram was acknowledged (ADR 0024). Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the Fragment's payload length in bytes; Value1 is this Reactor's ResolvedFragmentSize. Warn, for the same reason as DatagramMalformed: a remote can produce this at will. The handshake announces the size, so a conforming peer never sends a wider Fragment, and the width and the size say which end is misbuilt. PeerRefused = 300 A dialler was refused in-protocol during the stream handshake, either because it announced a different protocol version or because every capacity Slot was occupied. Subject is the claimed Source: at refusal time there is no Peer, only a claimed origin. For a capacity refusal, Value0 is this Reactor's capacity and Value1 is unused. For a version refusal, Value0 is the version offered and Value1 is the version this Reactor requires. Info, not Warn: a version mismatch on an upgrade and an ordinary burst at capacity are both routine, expected outcomes of running this profile, not conditions a consumer needs to act on. LingerNegotiated = 301 A Session established — on either profile, stream or datagram — and the two ends' announced Linger values were negotiated to their minimum (ADR 0011). Subject is the newly established Peer. Value0 is this end's own Linger in milliseconds; Value1 is the effective (minimum) Linger in milliseconds. MalformedFraming = 302 An established Peer's Message framing broke this profile's rules and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation: an oversized or zero-length prefix, or a stream that ended before a prefix or the Message body it named had fully arrived. Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the offending length prefix — 0 for a truncation, where no full prefix was ever read; Value1 is this Reactor's own MaxMessageSize. Warn: a remote can produce this at will by sending malformed bytes, which is exactly why the Session ends rather than throws, and why this is a Diagnostic rather than an Event on the consumer's own stream. DataAfterGoodbye = 303 An established Peer sent Message bytes after its own Goodbye had already been received, and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation. Subject is the Peer. Carries no claimed length — ReactorSockets.Session.MessageFramingLegality reaches this outcome before ever reading a prefix, so there is nothing to report but the contradiction itself. Value0 and Value1 are unused. Warn, for the same reason as MalformedFraming: a remote can produce this at will by ignoring the Goodbye it just sent. ResumeMatched = 304 A connection presenting a valid resume secret was matched onto the Interrupted Peer whose Slot was reserving the Session it named, and that Session continued over the replacement transport rather than a new one being established (ADR 0011). Subject is the resumed Peer — the same PeerId, generation included, the Session had before the interruption, since nothing about a Peer's identity is renewed by a Resume. Value0 is the number of retained outbound bytes the match rewound to the counter the Resume reported; Value1 is unused. On the datagram profile it is logged when a Resume control datagram matches the Peer on the accepting end (session id and secret), when an Interrupted accepting end receives a well-formed data Datagram for the Session from the exact address and port it sends to, and when an Interrupted dialling end that has sent a Resume hears its session again. Nothing is rewound, because retransmission already re-sends anything unacknowledged, so Value0 is 0 and Value1 is unused. Info: a reconnection is the outcome reserving a Slot exists to produce, not a condition a consumer needs to act on. Shared with the datagram session profile rather than duplicated in the datagram block, as are LingerNegotiated and ResumeUnmatched (ADR 0020). Numbered 304 because 302 and 303 belong to MalformedFraming and DataAfterGoodbye, and a value published in a closed permanent enum is never renumbered. ResumeUnmatched = 305 A connection claiming an existing Session was refused rather than resumed. Subject is the claimed Source: a claim that is not matched comes from a party that is by construction not a Peer, so there is no Peer to name, only a claimed origin. Value0 is the number of Interrupted Peers whose reservations the claim was checked against — 0 means nothing was being held at all, which is the reconfiguration path where a once-valid secret arrives after its Linger expired. Value1 is the wire record type the claim arrived as: 3 for a Resume whose secret matched no held Peer, and 1 for a Hello presenting a secret that did match, which re-announces the parameters a Resume has no field for and is refused as a protocol violation. Warn rather than the Info a version mismatch or a capacity refusal carries: those are routine outcomes of running this profile and a wrong secret is not. "Unmatched" names the outcome, not the comparison: the claim was not matched onto a Session. The Hello case reaches here having found the secret it announced, and is refused anyway because the record it arrived in re-announces parameters — Value1 is what tells the two apart. Value0 is reported to this end's own Sink and never to the wire: a refused party is closed on without being told anything, so it learns neither the count nor which of the three refusals it met. The datagram profile reports a Resume control datagram the same way, with Value1 6 (the Resume control type, DatagramControlType.Resume). Value0 is 0 when the target session id names no Peer the Reactor holds, or names a dialled Peer (never a Resume target, since only the dialling end sends Resume), and 1 when it names a Peer but the presented secret does not equal the one that Peer issued. RedialAttempted = 306 A dialling-side Peer began a fresh re-dial attempt after its transport was lost (ADR 0011). Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the attempt number, starting at 1 and rising by one per attempt; Value1 is the delay in milliseconds this attempt actually waited before dialling — the jittered figure ReactorSockets.Session.RedialSchedule.NextDelay() drew, so what actually elapsed is observable rather than only the computed figure before jitter. Info: a re-dial is the ordinary behaviour of a dialling Peer that lost its transport, not a condition a consumer needs to act on. RedialFailed = 307 A re-dial attempt could not connect, or connected and ended before the listener confirmed the Resume (ADR 0011). Subject is the Peer, which this never closes — it stays Interrupted and waits out the schedule's next delay, leaving Linger, not an attempt count, the only thing that ever closes it. Value0 carries the platform SocketError as its underlying integer value: for a connection that ended before confirmation it is Disconnecting for an end of stream, or the read's error. It is TimedOut when the listener did not answer within the receive-idle deadline, and SocketError when the Resume record could not be sent. Value1 is the attempt number that failed. Info rather than Warn: under this profile's premise a failed reconnection attempt is an ordinary, expected outcome, and raising it to Warn would train a consumer to ignore Warn. DeliveryCounterRefused = 308 An established Peer's delivery-counter record claimed to have received more Messages than this end has ever sent it, and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation — the peer is confirming Messages this end never queued, rather than merely repeating a count it already reported. Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the claimed cumulative count; Value1 is the count of Messages (and, if this end's own Goodbye has already been queued for this Peer, that too) this end has actually appended to this Peer's retention — the largest count a legitimate confirmation could ever sit at or below. Warn, for the same reason as MalformedFraming: a remote can produce this at will by inflating its own counter. Numbered 308 rather than the next free 304: ADR 0013's roster reserves 304-307 for the Resume and redial Diagnostics (ResumeMatched and ResumeUnmatched, then RedialAttempted and RedialFailed), and a value published in a closed permanent enum cannot be moved later to make room. Remarks Supported Sink style: range-check the blocks. The enum grows inside its blocks, so a Sink that classifies an id by the block it sits in, or that switches on members it cares about with a default arm for the rest, keeps working when a member is added. A Sink whose switch assumes it lists every member is not supported: the next additive release breaks it. A block names the profile that defined a condition, not the profile that emitted a record (ADR 0020). LingerNegotiated, ResumeMatched and ResumeUnmatched sit in the stream block and are emitted by the datagram session profile too, because each is one condition and a member names a condition. A Raw-only Sink's range check over 100-199 is exact, since nothing outside Raw shares that block. A Sink that needs to know which profile emitted a record knows which Reactor it was given to. Each member's documentation is the authority on its subject and value slots. ADR 0013's roster table is the one place to check them side by side and is kept in step with these docs.

Level The fixed severity for Id, per ADR 0013's roster. Link The Link this record concerns, valid only when SubjectKind is Link. Peer The Peer this record concerns, valid only when SubjectKind is Peer. Source The claimed Source this record concerns, valid only when SubjectKind is Source. SubjectKind Which of Link, Source or Peer, if any, is populated. Value0 The first numeric slot; meaning documented on the DiagnosticId member. ForAdmissionCapReached(int, int) Builds a AdmissionCapReached record. No subject. declined counts declinings where the work waits out of reach and pieces of work where the Reactor held it — see the remarks on AdmissionCapReached. ForArenaExhausted(LinkId, int, int) Builds an ArenaExhausted record for the Link that made the request. ForArenaExhausted(PeerId, int, int) Builds an ArenaExhausted record for the Peer whose Message could not be reserved — the Session profile's counterpart to the Link-subject overload above (ADR 0014: share-holder identity is per-Peer in a Session, not per-socket). ForCapacityExhausted(int, int) Builds a CapacityExhausted record. No subject. declined is counted exactly as ForAdmissionCapReached(int, int)'s is. ForCookieRejected(Source, long, long) Builds a CookieRejected record for the claimed Source, carrying the epoch the cookie offered and the epoch current when it was checked. ForDeliveryCounterRefused(PeerId, long, long) Builds a DeliveryCounterRefused record for the Peer whose delivery-counter record claimed more Messages than this end ever sent it. ForDestinationUnreachable(LinkId, SocketError) Builds a DestinationUnreachable record carrying the platform SocketError reported for the send. ForFragmentSetAbandoned(PeerId, long, long) Builds a FragmentSetAbandoned record for the Peer whose Fragment set was abandoned before it ever completed, carrying the fragments actually held and the number the set's own metadata declared. ForLingerNegotiated(PeerId, long, long) Builds a LingerNegotiated record for the newly established peer, on either profile — stream or datagram. Value0 is this end's own Linger in milliseconds; Value1 is the effective (minimum of the two ends') Linger in milliseconds. ForLinkFailed(LinkId, SocketError) Builds a LinkFailed record carrying the platform SocketError that caused the failure. ForMalformedFraming(PeerId, long, long) Builds a MalformedFraming record for the Peer whose framing broke this profile's rules. Value0 is the offending length prefix — 0 for a truncation, where no full prefix was ever read; Value1 is this Reactor's own MaxMessageSize. ForOversizedFragment(PeerId, long, long) Builds a OversizedFragment record for the Peer whose reliable Fragment was wider than this Reactor's own Fragment size, carrying the Fragment's payload length and that size. ForOversizedFragmentSet(PeerId, long, long) Builds a OversizedFragmentSet record for the Peer whose Fragment declared a fragmentCount larger than this Reactor's own receive window could ever hold, carrying the declared count and the largest legal count. ForOversizedMessage(PeerId, long, long) Builds a OversizedMessage record for the Peer whose completed Message was larger than this Reactor's own MaxMessageSize, carrying the Message's length and that limit. ForPeerRefusedCapacity(Source, int) Builds a PeerRefused record for the claimed Source of a stream dialler refused because every capacity Slot was occupied. Value0 carries this Reactor's capacity; Value1 is unused. ForPeerRefusedVersion(Source, long, long) Builds a PeerRefused record for the claimed Source of a stream dialler refused because it announced a version this Reactor does not speak. ReactorSockets.DiagnosticSubjectKind.htm.summary: Enum DiagnosticSubjectKind Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Which field of a DiagnosticRecord's tagged subject is populated (ADR 0013). A record has exactly one subject, so a Sink or formatter switches on this rather than checking several optional fields for which one is set. public enum DiagnosticSubjectKind Fields None = 0 The record concerns no particular Link or Source. Link = 1 The record concerns a registered Link, carried in Link. Source = 2 The record concerns an unauthenticated claimed origin, carried in Source. Peer = 3 The record concerns an established Peer, carried in Peer. Distinct from Source: a Peer exists only once a handshake has completed, while a Source is merely a claimed origin — a refusal made before a Peer exists tags Source, never this.

ReactorSockets.DisconnectReason.html.title: Enum DisconnectReason | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DisconnectReason.html.summary: Enum DisconnectReason Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Why a Peer's Session ended, defined and kept stable by this library rather than borrowed from a platform enumeration. Deliberately not shared with the Raw profile's CloseReason (ADR 0008): most of the members a Session needs are protocol vocabulary Raw can never produce, and a single shared enumeration would leave one profile documenting members it cannot emit. public enum DisconnectReason Fields LocalClose = 0 The consumer called Close on this Peer. In the datagram profile this also ends a Peer whose own Close was in progress when the remote's Goodbye arrived: when both ends close at once, each reports this and neither reports PeerGoodbye. VersionMismatch = 1 The two ends do not speak the same protocol version. The version match is exact — there is no negotiation, no lowest-common-version rule and no compatibility range — so this is produced both by the end that refused and by the end whose Hello was refused. RemoteAtCapacity = 2 The remote end had no capacity Slot free for this Session and said so. Distinct from silence: a Reactor at capacity answers a Hello it received rather than dropping it, so the dialler learns the difference between "full" and "gone". It also means this address may be at the far end's MaxPeersPerAddress or MaxPeersPerAddress, so other Slots may be free. TransportFailed = 3 The underlying transport failed or ended before or during the handshake: a reset, a dial that could not connect, or a stream that closed before a full handshake record arrived. Distinct from every other member here because nothing about the protocol was at fault — the byte stream itself did not survive to carry it. The same kind of failure on an established Peer does not produce this reason at all — it moves the Peer to PeerInterrupted instead, because its identity and undelivered Messages are still worth holding for a Resume. This member now fires only for a Peer that never finished becoming one. The datagram profile has no transport to fail, and produces this member for a dial that got no answer: one still pending its own Linger after Connect(IPEndPoint), its handshake resent throughout (ADR 0009, amendment of 2026-11-10). ProtocolViolation = 4 An established Peer's Message framing broke this profile's rules: a length prefix exceeding the announced MaxMessageSize, a length prefix of zero, a stream that ended before a length prefix or the Message body it named had fully arrived, or bytes arriving behind a Goodbye already received from that Peer — a Peer that announced it was leaving and then kept sending is contradicting its own announcement, so it is disconnected rather than believed. On the stream profile it also ends a dial the far end refused for sending more than one further handshake record's worth of bytes behind its first record before it was answered. Distinct from TransportFailed: the byte stream itself survived long enough to carry the violation, and what is wrong is the bytes it carried rather than the transport underneath it. Distinct from PeerGoodbye, which is reserved for an ending that stayed clean to the last byte. PeerGoodbye = 5 The remote Peer sent a Goodbye: it is ending the Session on purpose rather than failing. Produced once whatever this end still held for it has finished flushing — immediately, if nothing was outstanding when the Goodbye arrived, or after the Closing Session it entered (PeerClosing) has drained. The datagram profile raises it the same way, once the Goodbye reaches its turn in ReliableOrdered send order, except that a Peer whose own Close is already in progress acknowledges the Goodbye and ends with LocalClose instead. LingerExpired = 6 An PeerInterrupted Peer's effective Linger — the value LingerNegotiated already reported at handshake (ADR 0011), the minimum of the two ends' announced Lingers — elapsed before the transport came back (stream profile, datagram profile). Linger, not the loss of the transport, is what closes an Interrupted Peer: the loss itself only produced PeerInterrupted and held the Peer's identity, counters and undelivered Messages open for a Resume. This member fires once that wait has run out, and is also what bounds a Close(PeerId) whose Goodbye can never reach a wire that no longer exists — without it, that Peer's retention would sit pending forever. Distinct from TransportFailed, which means the byte stream never survived long enough to say anything at all — this means it survived, said nothing further within the time this end had promised to wait, and this end gave up on its own clock rather than being told to. Distinct from PeerGoodbye, which is an ending the remote announced on purpose while its transport still worked — this is an ending this end declares unilaterally, after silence, with no announcement possible because the transport that would have carried one is already gone. The datagram profile (DatagramSessionReactor) has no socket to lose, so an Interrupted datagram Peer's own HasLingerExpired reads the same PeerSlot.EffectiveLinger against PeerSlot.InterruptedTimestamp — the Pump that set PeerSlot.IsInterrupted, never re-stamped while it continues — that the stream profile's HasExceededLinger reads against its own equivalent timestamp, and this member is what that per-Pump pass produces once the wait runs out. Everything else this member's summary says about Linger governing the close, not the transport loss that produced the interruption, holds identically for both profiles. A datagram Peer in Closing (Close(PeerId)) also ends with this reason when its Goodbye is still unacknowledged once its effective Linger has elapsed since Close. RetentionGap = 7 A Resume's reported delivery counter named a Message position below this end's retention ring — the peer confirmed nothing further, but by the time it reconnected the bytes at its reported position had already been released to make room for newer ones (RetentionExhausted during the interruption). Resuming anyway would deliver a stream with a hole in it, so this end closes instead. Distinct from LingerExpired and TransportFailed because both of those are silent about why the Session ended — nothing was wrong with what either side said, only with how long the transport stayed reachable — while this one is a direct statement about what the peer said: its retention window was too small for the outage it just had. That makes the remedy actionable and specific — raise this end's retention capacity or its Linger, or both — in a way neither of those two members is. The mirror case, a Resume counter naming a Message this end never sent at all, is not this member: that is a protocol violation (ProtocolViolation), not a capacity question, because no amount of retention would have made a fabricated counter valid. FragmentSizeUnviable = 8 The configured fragment size (FragmentSize) is larger than this network path will carry. Detected from the fragment-size stall signature (ReactorSockets.FragmentStallSignature.IsFragmentSizeStall): unfragmented reliable records kept being acknowledged — proving the path and this Peer are both reachable — while not one Fragment was acknowledged across ReactorSockets.FragmentStallSignature.StallRoundCount retransmission rounds, which is only explained by every Fragment being lost every round because of its size rather than by chance. The remedy is to lower FragmentSize; nothing this library can change fixes it, since the configuration itself is what will not fit. This member is a diagnosis, not a fault this end tries to work around: no probe datagram is sent, no fragment size is reduced, nothing smaller is retried, and the Session simply closes with this reason. Each of those would mean measuring a path this library deliberately declines to probe (ADR 0004) and replacing a size the consumer configured with one this library guessed, so recovery is left entirely to the consumer changing their own configuration and reconnecting. A Message already cut into Fragments keeps the size it was cut at, because fragment size is fixed at Send(PeerId, DeliveryMode, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) and retransmits are byte-identical. Distinct from TransportFailed and LingerExpired, both of which are silent about why the Session ended — nothing here said anything was wrong with the bytes, only that the transport stopped answering — while this member is a direct statement about what was observed: unfragmented traffic proved the path alive while every Fragment vanished. Distinct from RetentionGap, the other member whose remedy is a configuration change: that one names a capacity too small for an outage already survived, this one names a size too large for the path carrying it. Named for the setting that cannot work, FragmentSize, rather than for the stall that revealed it, because the stall is only the symptom and the fragment size is what the consumer can actually change. Remarks Explicit values throughout, house style since RawLinkLegality: a member is added at the end with the next free number, never inserted, so a value a consumer has already persisted keeps its meaning across a library upgrade. Every place this library maps something else onto a DisconnectReason — a wire ReactorSockets.Session.RefusalReason, a malformed-framing outcome, a Goodbye control record — states that mapping as its own table with a discard arm that refuses rather than permits, the same house rule RawLinkLegality follows: an input this library does not recognise fails closed instead of being guessed at.

Not derivable: the Reactor-scope datagram figures count datagrams rather than bytes, cover every Link at once, and never see a stream Link. ReactorSockets.LinkId.-ctor.html.title: Constructor LinkId | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.LinkId.-ctor.html.summary: Constructor LinkId Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll LinkId(uint, int, ulong) A Link's identity: the Reactor that issued it, a zero-based slot index, and a generation counter that increments when the slot is reused, so a stale LinkId held past a Link's close compares unequal to whatever now occupies that slot (ADR 0014) rather than aliasing it. public LinkId(uint Origin, int Index, ulong Generation) Parameters Origin uint Which Reactor issued this LinkId. Opaque and process-local — compared for equality and nothing else, ordering nothing and meaning nothing outside this process. Never 0: that value is reserved and no Reactor is ever issued it, so a default LinkId addresses nothing twice over. Index int The zero-based Slot this Link occupies. Generation ulong The generation that Slot was on when this Link was admitted. Live Slots begin at 1, so a default LinkId — generation 0 — addresses nothing. Remarks The generation is ulong rather than int so that it cannot wrap within the life of any process, which is what lets generation 0 stay a reserved sentinel without a check guarding it. ADR 0015 records the reasoning and the alternatives declined. The Origin extends that same guarantee across Reactors. Index and generation are unique only within one Reactor's table, and every table's first Link is Slot 0 generation 1, so without it a LinkId from one RawReactor addressed a live Link of another.

ReactorSockets.Logging.LoggerSink.-ctor..title: Constructor LoggerSink | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.Logging.LoggerSink.-ctor..summary: Constructor LoggerSink Namespace ReactorSockets.Logging Assembly ReactorSockets.Logging.dll LoggerSink(ILogger) An IReactorDiagnostics Sink that writes each record to an ILogger. The message is Format(in DiagnosticRecord)'s text, never wording of this package's own, and the state carries the record's typed fields for a structured provider. One type serves every profile: install one per Reactor, each over a logger with its own category from one ILoggerFactory, and every Reactor writes one stream with each record attributed by category. public LoggerSink(ILogger logger) Parameters logger ILogger The logger every record is written to. Remarks This Sink is bound by the same contract as any other (ADR 0005): the Reactor calls it synchronously, on the thread that called Pump, inside the Frame. Every provider the ILogger is wired to runs there too, so a provider that writes to a console or a file synchronously stalls the Frame for as long as the write takes. Configure providers that hand the write off and return. The category is the attribution. A record with a Link or Peer subject also names its Reactor in the Reactor field and the message, but a record with no subject or a Source subject names none, so one instance shared between Reactors leaves those unattributed.

This is what makes a share exhaustion visible: a Frame in which bytes plainly arrived but this figure did not move is a Message still buffered, not one dropped. Not derivable: byte figures include framing and handshake bytes and say nothing of how many Messages they carried. RetentionHighWaterBytes ulong The most bytes this Peer's retention ring has ever held at once (written minus released) since the Peer was established — HighWaterBytes(int) read fresh at snapshot time, never pushed. Monotonic for the Peer's lifetime: draining the ring after a burst lowers what is currently retained but never lowers this figure. Not derivable: bytes sent is a running total, and how much of it was unacknowledged at once is what sizes retention. Resumes ulong How many times this Peer's transport has been successfully resumed after an Interruption (ADR 0013). Incremented once per PeerResumed raised for this Peer, on both the listening and dialling sides, and never on a refused resume. Earns its own member rather than being derived by the consumer counting PeerResumed Events: a Session profile drains Events into whatever cadence the consumer chooses, so counting them back out is not generally possible once drained, while this figure is a Counter — read fresh by value at any time, the same as every other figure here. Monotonic and never reset: a resume carries no counter's history away with it, so a retransmission count spanning several resumes is how a flapping path shows itself instead of being hidden by a zeroing on every reconnect. Not derivable: no other counter moves only on a Resume. OutOfWindowPackets ulong How many packet records this Peer's per-Space receive window has classified as out of window — a sequence number too far ahead of, or behind, that Space's receive window base to be tracked against it (ADR 0013). Recurs every Pump under sustained loss or reordering, which is exactly why it is a Counter and never a Diagnostic. Incremented by the parse loop's classification of each arriving record; a freshly connected Peer reads zero. Note that only the two reliable Spaces raise this on a far-ahead arrival: the unreliable Spaces slide their window forward instead and count the retirement as loss, so for those Spaces out-of-window means a sequence below the base alone. A ReliableOrdered record the window would admit but the Space will not hold behind a gap counts here too, because it is refused the same way and comes back by retransmission. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: bytes received counts these records together with admitted ones, and no other figure separates reordering beyond the window from repeats. DuplicatePackets ulong How many packet records this Peer's per-Space receive window has classified as duplicates — a sequence number already accounted for, most often a retransmission the far end sent because it never saw this end's acknowledgement rather than a protocol violation (ADR 0013). Recurs every Pump under sustained loss exactly like OutOfWindowPackets, and for the same reason is a Counter. Incremented by the parse loop's classification of each arriving record; a freshly connected Peer reads zero. The plain Unreliable Space contributes from a second place as well (ADR 0017): that Space suppresses repeats within its own bounded 64-sequence window, a protocol constant rather than the receive window, and a repeat that window catches after the receive window admitted it raises this figure. A repeat the receive window itself refused is counted there instead — most often on OutOfWindowPackets, since a repeat usually arrives below a base that has already passed it — so one record raises one figure and never both. A repeat delayed past those 64 sequences is delivered and raises neither: suppression there is bounded by design, and these figures count what was refused rather than what was repeated. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: this end's retransmissions are PacketsRetransmitted, and only this figure sees the far end's, from the receiving side. UnreliableLossPackets ulong How many sequences an unreliable Space's receive window has lost — retired by sliding its base forward before that sequence ever arrived (ADR 0013). A gap is provisional until the window passes it by: a sequence still inside the window may yet arrive late and be admitted without ever touching this figure, so it reflects only sequences a window has moved past, never every sequence not yet seen. This is one figure covering both unreliable Spaces — Unreliable and UnreliableSequenced — summed, exactly as OutOfWindowPackets and DuplicatePackets already cover all four Spaces summed, so per-Space loss is not separable from it. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: a sequence that never arrives is never classified, so no other figure can see it. It measures a deferral, not a loss: the sequence is not missing and nothing was discarded, only judged too far ahead of [base, base + 32] for this Pump's ack blocks to describe yet, so the timer that would otherwise start ticking toward a spurious retransmission is withheld until the horizon slides over it. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like OutOfWindowPackets: a Resume carries no counter's history away with it, and this one's lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's. Not derivable: these sequences were admitted, so no refusal figure counts them, and only this one says the ack horizon was outrun. Counts packet RECORDS resent, not datagrams sent and not Messages: retransmission is byte-identical at packet- record granularity, because a datagram is repacked on every send and is not itself reproducible — several records can ride one datagram, and the same record can ride a different datagram on retry. Not derivable: the Reactor-scope datagram figures count datagrams for every Peer at once and lose closed Peers, and the stream profile has no other byte figure. Incremented once per data Datagram that both names an established Peer's session id and proves well-formed — the same proof that gates ack application and record classification — at the whole Datagram's length, header included, mirroring BytesSent. A Datagram naming no Session, or one so malformed it cannot be attributed to the Peer it claims, charges no Peer: it lands on a Reactor-scope figure instead. The first record on an accepted connection is charged once it is admitted as this Peer or matched as its Resume. A connection refused or never matched charges no Peer. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like HorizonDeferrals: its lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's, so a Resume does not zero it. A freshly connected datagram Peer reads zero.
