Monotonic and never reset, exactly like HorizonDeferrals: its lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's, so a Resume does not zero it. A freshly connected datagram Peer reads zero. Not derivable: MessagesReceived counts Messages rather than bytes, and the Reactor-scope figures neither attribute bytes to a Peer nor see a stream connection. BytesSent On the datagram profile, the datagram bytes a flush has handed the transport for this Peer, header included (ADR 0013). Incremented once per Datagram, at the size the coalescing packer actually wrote for it — the 20-byte session header plus every packet record's own header and payload — rather than per record or per payload byte, since header bytes amortising across a Pump's coalesced records is exactly what this figure exists to let a consumer see; counting payload alone would hide that amortisation. Raised regardless of whether the underlying send call reports success, since the bytes were handed to the transport at that point either way — distinct from the Reactor-scope send figure, which counts only a confirmed success. A data Datagram to an Established Peer moves this, and so does each Resume control datagram the dialling end sends it, at its fixed 256 bytes, because a Peer exists to charge. A handshake's control datagrams carry no session id yet to attribute them to, so they are never counted here, on either the sent or the received side (see BytesReceived). On the stream profile, the bytes the socket accepted on this Peer's connection, framing included: every write a Peer is charged a SocketWrites for, handshake and Resume records too, at the count each call reported written. A short write counts the part that went. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like HorizonDeferrals: its lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's, so a Resume does not zero it. Not derivable: the Reactor-scope datagram figures count datagrams for every Peer at once and lose closed Peers, and the stream profile has no other byte figure. DuplicatePackets How many packet records this Peer's per-Space receive window has classified as duplicates — a sequence number already accounted for, most often a retransmission the far end sent because it never saw this end's acknowledgement rather than a protocol violation (ADR 0013). Recurs every Pump under sustained loss exactly like OutOfWindowPackets, and for the same reason is a Counter. Incremented by the parse loop's classification of each arriving record; a freshly connected Peer reads zero. The plain Unreliable Space contributes from a second place as well (ADR 0017): that Space suppresses repeats within its own bounded 64-sequence window, a protocol constant rather than the receive window, and a repeat that window catches after the receive window admitted it raises this figure. A repeat the receive window itself refused is counted there instead — most often on OutOfWindowPackets, since a repeat usually arrives below a base that has already passed it — so one record raises one figure and never both. A repeat delayed past those 64 sequences is delivered and raises neither: suppression there is bounded by design, and these figures count what was refused rather than what was repeated. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: this end's retransmissions are PacketsRetransmitted, and only this figure sees the far end's, from the receiving side. HorizonDeferrals How many sequences arrived beyond a reliable Space's ack horizon and so had their retransmit timer withheld rather than started (ADR 0013). It measures a deferral, not a loss: the sequence is not missing and nothing was discarded, only judged too far ahead of [base, base + 32] for this Pump's ack blocks to describe yet, so the timer that would otherwise start ticking toward a spurious retransmission is withheld until the horizon slides over it. This is why it is a Counter and not a Diagnostic (ADR 0013): sustained load with many sequences in flight defers on every Pump, which fails the record test, and it keeps its own identity — rather than folding into OutOfWindowPackets — because counters have a per-Peer scope. Only the two reliable Spaces contribute; the unreliable Spaces have no ack horizon to sit beyond. Rises only under the horizon scenario and stays zero in ordinary operation, where every sequence lands inside the horizon as it arrives. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like OutOfWindowPackets: a Resume carries no counter's history away with it, and this one's lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's. A freshly connected Peer reads zero. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: these sequences were admitted, so no refusal figure counts them, and only this one says the ack horizon was outrun. MessagesReceived Whole Messages handed to the frame arena for delivery — incremented at that point only, never when a Message's bytes finish arriving or while it sits buffered waiting for a read share or arena room. This is what makes a share exhaustion visible: a Frame in which bytes plainly arrived but this figure did not move is a Message still buffered, not one dropped. Not derivable: byte figures include framing and handshake bytes and say nothing of how many Messages they carried. OutOfWindowPackets How many packet records this Peer's per-Space receive window has classified as out of window — a sequence number too far ahead of, or behind, that Space's receive window base to be tracked against it (ADR 0013). Recurs every Pump under sustained loss or reordering, which is exactly why it is a Counter and never a Diagnostic. Incremented by the parse loop's classification of each arriving record; a freshly connected Peer reads zero. Note that only the two reliable Spaces raise this on a far-ahead arrival: the unreliable Spaces slide their window forward instead and count the retirement as loss, so for those Spaces out-of-window means a sequence below the base alone. A ReliableOrdered record the window would admit but the Space will not hold behind a gap counts here too, because it is refused the same way and comes back by retransmission. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: bytes received counts these records together with admitted ones, and no other figure separates reordering beyond the window from repeats. PacketsRetransmitted How many packet records this Peer has resent (ADR 0013). Counts packet RECORDS resent, not datagrams sent and not Messages: retransmission is byte-identical at packet- record granularity, because a datagram is repacked on every send and is not itself reproducible — several records can ride one datagram, and the same record can ride a different datagram on retry. This is why it is a Counter and not a Diagnostic (ADR 0013): a retransmit recurs continuously on a lossy path, which fails the record test, and it keeps its own identity — rather than folding into OutOfWindowPackets or HorizonDeferrals — because counters have a per-Peer scope. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like HorizonDeferrals: its lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's, so a Resume does not zero it. Raised by the retransmit expiry sweep; a freshly connected Peer reads zero. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: bytes sent mixes first sends with resends, and only this figure separates them. ReadShareExhaustions How many times this Peer had a whole Message ready and was refused Arena room because it had already used its read share for the Frame (ADR 0013, where ReadShareReached became this counter). Counted once per refused reservation. What becomes of the Message differs by profile. The stream profile keeps it buffered and delivers it on a later Pump. On the datagram profile an unreliable record is lost. A reliable one is delivered on a later Pump: a record still held for send order or reassembly is retried from where it is held, and any other is left unacknowledged so the far end retransmits it. Recurs every Pump while one Peer outpaces its share, which is why it is a Counter and not a Diagnostic. Moves on both Session profiles. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like HorizonDeferrals: its lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's, so a Resume does not zero it. Not derivable: bytes received and MessagesReceived show that delivery lagged arrival, but not that the read share was the cause rather than the Arena itself running out. Resumes How many times this Peer's transport has been successfully resumed after an Interruption (ADR 0013). Incremented once per PeerResumed raised for this Peer, on both the listening and dialling sides, and never on a refused resume. Earns its own member rather than being derived by the consumer counting PeerResumed Events: a Session profile drains Events into whatever cadence the consumer chooses, so counting them back out is not generally possible once drained, while this figure is a Counter — read fresh by value at any time, the same as every other figure here. Monotonic and never reset: a resume carries no counter's history away with it, so a retransmission count spanning several resumes is how a flapping path shows itself instead of being hidden by a zeroing on every reconnect. Not derivable: no other counter moves only on a Resume. RetentionHighWaterBytes The most bytes this Peer's retention ring has ever held at once (written minus released) since the Peer was established — HighWaterBytes(int) read fresh at snapshot time, never pushed. Monotonic for the Peer's lifetime: draining the ring after a burst lowers what is currently retained but never lowers this figure. Not derivable: bytes sent is a running total, and how much of it was unacknowledged at once is what sizes retention. SocketWrites How many socket send calls this Reactor has made on this Peer's transport (ADR 0013). One per call, whatever it carried and however it ended — a whole write, a short write and a failed call each count once — because the figure measures what the Reactor paid in syscalls, not what the socket accepted. On the stream profile every write on the Peer's connection counts: handshake and Resume records, delivery-counter records sent alone, and each retention write, where a delivery counter riding that write adds nothing. On the datagram profile it counts one per data Datagram a flush hands the transport and one per Resume control datagram the dialling end sends, beside BytesSent; a handshake's control datagrams are never counted, for the same reason they never reach BytesSent. A rate well above the Pump rate for one Peer names a write path that is not batching. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like HorizonDeferrals: its lifetime is the Peer's, not the transport's, so a Resume does not zero it. Not derivable: how many bytes went out says nothing about how many calls carried them. UnreliableLossPackets How many sequences an unreliable Space's receive window has lost — retired by sliding its base forward before that sequence ever arrived (ADR 0013). A gap is provisional until the window passes it by: a sequence still inside the window may yet arrive late and be admitted without ever touching this figure, so it reflects only sequences a window has moved past, never every sequence not yet seen. This is one figure covering both unreliable Spaces — Unreliable and UnreliableSequenced — summed, exactly as OutOfWindowPackets and DuplicatePackets already cover all four Spaces summed, so per-Space loss is not separable from it. The two reliable Spaces never contribute, because their windows do not slide: retransmission is what fills their holes, and what they refuse lands on OutOfWindowPackets instead. No Diagnostic accompanies a gap in either Space; a lossy path must not fill the Sink with volume. Monotonic and never reset, exactly like OutOfWindowPackets; a freshly connected Peer reads zero. Moves only on the datagram profile. Not derivable: a sequence that never arrives is never classified, so no other figure can see it.

ReactorSockets.PeerId.-ctor.html.title: Constructor PeerId | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.PeerId.-ctor.html.summary: Constructor PeerId Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll PeerId(uint, int, ulong) A Peer's identity inside this process: the Reactor that issued it, a zero-based Slot index, and a generation counter that increments when the Slot is reused, so a stale PeerId held past a Peer's close compares unequal to whatever now occupies that Slot (ADR 0007) rather than aliasing it. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010), exactly as LinkId is the Raw profile's. public PeerId(uint Origin, int Index, ulong Generation) Parameters Origin uint Which Reactor issued this PeerId. Opaque and process-local — it is compared for equality and nothing else, orders nothing, and never appears on the wire. Never 0: that value is reserved and no Reactor is ever issued it, so a default PeerId addresses nothing twice over. Not a Source, which names a remote address; this names a Reactor of this process. Index int The zero-based Slot this Peer occupies. Generation ulong The generation that Slot was on when this Peer was admitted. Live Slots begin at 1, so a default PeerId — generation 0 — addresses nothing. Remarks This is deliberately not the identity a datagram Session puts on the wire. A Slot index is dense, small and guessable, and a remote that can guess one can address a Peer it was never introduced to; the wire identity is instead a receiver-assigned random 32-bit value the two ends exchange during the handshake, and it never appears on this type. The generation is ulong rather than int so that it cannot wrap within the life of any process, which is what lets generation 0 stay a reserved sentinel without a check guarding it (ADR 0015). The Origin is what makes a PeerId mean something to exactly one Reactor. Without it, index and generation are only unique within a single Reactor's table, and every table's first Peer is Slot 0 generation 1 — so one Reactor's PeerId passed to another's Close named a live Peer of that second Reactor and closed it. A consumer running two Reactors gets the mistake back as nothing happening, which is what an id addressing no Peer has always meant here.

ReactorSockets.RawEventKind.html.summary: Enum RawEventKind Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Which kind of RawEvent a drained event is (ADR 0008). Accepted comes from a listening Link, Connected from dialling, SegmentReceived and EndOfStream from stream reads, and Writable from partial sends. public enum RawEventKind Fields DatagramReceived = 0 A datagram arrived on a bound UDP Link. Link, Source and Payload are populated. Closed = 1 A Link closed. Link and Reason are populated. Accepted = 2 A connection was accepted on a listening Link, inside the Pump that found it ready. ListeningLink names the listening Link that fired; Link names the new connection, already registered and consuming a capacity slot of its own. Connected = 3 An outbound dial completed successfully, inside the Pump that found the connecting socket writable. Link is populated; a dial that fails instead produces Closed with Refused or Unreachable. SegmentReceived = 4 A run of bytes arrived on a stream Link. Link and Payload are populated. Carries no claim of being a whole anything — a counterparty's single write may be drained as one or several of these, and framing is the consumer's decision, not this library's. EndOfStream = 5 The remote end of a stream Link will send nothing further while this Link remains open for sending — TCP's own half-close, kept separate from Closed because collapsing them would decide on the consumer's behalf that their protocol cannot use half-close. Link is populated. A consumer that never calls Close after this holds the Link and its slot until the Reactor is disposed — there is no Linger in Raw to reclaim it. Writable = 6 A stream Link that took fewer bytes than offered on a previous Send has become writable again. Link is populated. Armed, not level-triggered: exactly one of these follows a short send, and a Link never over-sent on produces none at all — a reply to something the consumer did, not a status the Reactor volunteers every Pump a socket happens to be writable (which is nearly always).

ReactorSockets.RawReactor.-ctor.html.summary: Constructor RawReactor Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll RawReactor(ReactorOptions, int?) Constructs a Reactor bound to the calling thread (ADR 0002) — every future mutating call must come from this same thread or it throws. public RawReactor(ReactorOptions options, int? scratchBufferSize = null) Parameters options ReactorOptions The shared options value. Every knob on it is validated here, and ArenaSize is resolved against this profile's floor; a combination that cannot work throws at construction and nowhere else. scratchBufferSize int? The single scratch buffer every Link's receive lands in, reused across Links since only one is read at any instant inside a single-threaded Pump (ADR 0012). Defaults to MaxUdpDatagramSize. Provenance: the largest payload a UDP datagram can carry over IPv4, at which an IPv4 datagram cannot be truncated. An IPv6 datagram of 65 508 to 65 527 bytes exceeds it and is reported as truncated. This is the profile-specific knob a consumer lowers to opt into truncation, kept off ReactorOptions because it has no meaning outside Raw's datagram surface. Remarks The memory bill is one scratch buffer plus one arena — scratchBufferSize + 1 + ArenaSize (the extra byte is how a truncated datagram is recognised) — neither multiplied by capacity, because Raw holds nothing for a Link across a Pump. That is what "invents nothing on the wire" looks like from the constructor (ADR 0012).

ReactorSockets.RawReactor.Listen.html.summary: Method Listen Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Listen(IPEndPoint) Binds and listens on a new TCP socket at endpoint, returning the LinkId that addresses it. A listening socket is a Link like any other — one identity type, one lifecycle, one Closed event — because "Listener" is a role a Link plays for a consumer, not a kind of thing this library names (ADR 0008). ReactorSockets.SendOutcome.html.summary: Enum SendOutcome Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll The outcome of one Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) call. A bare enum rather than a result struct (unlike SendResult): a Session-level send has no partial-completion quantity worth reporting back — the framed Message either fit in the Peer's retention region whole, or it did not, so the outcome is the whole story. public enum SendOutcome Fields Sent = 0 The framed Message was copied whole into the Peer's retention region. RetentionExhausted = 1 The Peer's retention region had no room for the framed Message. Nothing was copied and nothing about the Session changed — the caller may retry once bytes have been released, or otherwise. Closed = 2 A Goodbye for this Peer has already passed in one direction or the other — this end sent its own (Close), or the far end's arrived and the Peer is Closing. Either way the Session is ending and nothing was copied: a Message queued after a Goodbye would have to either jump it in retention or follow it, and neither is a Message the far end has any business receiving. MessageTooLarge = 3 The Message is wider than one Datagram can carry, and the Space it was sent on cannot fragment it. On the datagram profile that cap is the Peer's send Fragment size: the smaller of this end's ResolvedFragmentSize and the Fragment size the peer announced (ADR 0024). Nothing was copied. Deliberately its own value rather than folded into RetentionExhausted: retention exhaustion is backpressure the caller can retry once bytes are released, while an oversized Message will never fit however long the caller waits — a consumer that cannot tell the two apart cannot tell "retry later" from "split it or use a reliable mode". RemoteMessageTooLarge = 4 A Message, in any delivery mode, exceeds the MaxMessageSize the remote end announced during the handshake, or a reliable Message needs more Fragments than the receive window the remote end announced (ADR 0024). Nothing was copied, and the caller may retry immediately with a smaller payload. An unreliable Message over both limits reports MessageTooLarge instead. Distinct from MessageTooLarge by which limit was exceeded: that value means the single-Datagram cap an unreliable mode cannot exceed, which a smaller peer Fragment size lowers; this one means the far end's announced receive limit, its MaxMessageSize or its receive window. NotEstablished = 5 The Peer's handshake has not completed: a dial is still connecting, or waiting for the far end's handshake record. Nothing was copied and nothing about the Session changed. Wait for PeerConnected for this Peer before Sending. Refusing here rather than queueing keeps a Message from reaching a socket whose connect has not resolved, or going out before this end knows the far end's version and announced MaxMessageSize. Remarks Deliberately its own type rather than folded into DisconnectReason: exhausting retention does not end the Session, so it belongs on the return of the call that can produce it rather than mixed into the roster of reasons a Peer is gone. Explicit values throughout, the same house style as DisconnectReason: a member is added at the end with the next free number, never inserted, so a value a consumer has already persisted keeps its meaning across a library upgrade.

ReactorSockets.SessionEventKind.html.title: Enum SessionEventKind | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.SessionEventKind.html.summary: Enum SessionEventKind Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Which kind of SessionEvent was drained, and therefore which of its fields carry meaning. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010). public enum SessionEventKind Fields PeerConnected = 1 A Session is established and the Peer is addressable. Raised on both ends: on the dialler when the Accept arrives, on the accepting end when a Hello is admitted. PeerClosed = 2 A Session ended, or a dial never became one. Reason says why, and the PeerId is dead from this event onwards. MessageReceived = 3 A whole Message was reassembled from the Peer's stream and copied into the frame arena. Payload carries it, valid only until the next Pump (ADR 0008). PeerClosing = 4 The Peer's Goodbye arrived while something was still outstanding to deliver: either Messages this end had already reassembled from it but the consumer had not yet drained (even though it reached MessageReceived first), or bytes still buffered in its receive share awaiting arena room, or this end's own outbound retention for it still being flushed to the socket. The Peer accepts no further Sends worth making from here and a PeerClosed carrying PeerGoodbye follows once all of that is exhausted. Never raised when nothing was outstanding on either side — a Goodbye that finds the Peer already caught up closes it directly, with no zero-Frame Closing observable in between. In the datagram profile the Goodbye acts at its turn in ReliableOrdered send order, and "outstanding" means Messages received but not yet delivered. PeerInterrupted = 5 The stream profile's transport for this Peer is gone, but the Peer itself is not: its PeerId — including generation — stays live, CountersOf(PeerId) keeps answering for it, and its undelivered inbound Messages and outbound retention ring are held rather than discarded (ADR 0010). Raised whenever an established Peer's transport ends without a Goodbye first: an inbound FIN carrying nothing further, a reset, a local write failure, or this end's own receive-idle deadline expiring (which closed the Peer outright before this kind existed). Distinct from PeerClosing: Closing means a Goodbye arrived and the Session is ending on purpose, with PeerClosed to follow once both sides drain — nothing here is ever resumable. Interrupted means the opposite — no Goodbye was ever seen, the Session is not ending, and the Peer sits ready for a Resume for as long as Linger allows. A Peer that sent Goodbye and then a bare FIN reaches PeerClosing or PeerClosed, never this. Carries only Peer — there is no DisconnectReason to report, because nothing has ended. PeerResumed = 6 A Session held PeerInterrupted reclaimed its transport and is delivering again. Raised on whichever side completes the match, and in both cases only once that side knows where to resend from: on the listening side from ResumeHeldPeer, once the peer's Resume record checks out and its carried delivery counter has driven the rewind; on the dialling side not from ResumeDialledPeer, which only sends the Resume record, but later, when the listening side's reciprocal delivery-counter record arrives and is rewound off. Only that success path reaches here: a resume refused because the peer named a Message this end no longer retains closes the Peer instead (RetentionGap) and never raises this. Peer's PeerId, generation included, is exactly the one PeerInterrupted carried — a Resume is the same Peer's transport coming back, never a new one — and no PeerClosed is ever observed between the two. The consumer is asked for no reconciliation: Messages sent before the interruption arrive without being re-sent, since the rewind that makes this event possible already put this end's outbound retention back to the peer's last confirmed point before this event is raised. Carries only Peer, the same as PeerInterrupted — nothing has ended, so there is no DisconnectReason to report. Remarks Members are appended, never inserted.

The PeerClosed carrying LocalClose is queued once that flush fully drains — immediately, on a later Pump, if nothing was queued when Close(PeerId) was called, or after however many Pumps a short write (or a retention append retry) takes to carry everything already retained plus the Goodbye itself. Every Peer whose received count advanced somewhere in that work — this Frame's own reads, or a held-back Message finally delivered by ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.RetryPeersWithBufferedMessages() — then has its delivery counter emitted exactly once (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.EmitDeliveryCounters()), before every Peer's queued retention bytes are flushed exactly once (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.FlushPendingRetentionWrites()) regardless of how many Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) calls queued them. Finally, every established Peer's two independent idle timers are enforced in one scan (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.EnforceIdleTimers()): a Peer from which nothing has been received for ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot.RemoteSendIdleInterval × ResolvedMissedHeartbeats moves to PeerInterrupted, an already-Interrupted Peer instead closes with LingerExpired once its effective Linger has elapsed since the interruption, and every surviving Peer that has written nothing to the wire — including whatever this Frame's own flush just carried — for at least SendIdleInterval sends the same delivery-counter record as a heartbeat, unconditionally and regardless of whether anything was ever received from it. Once idle timers may have closed an Interrupted Peer on Linger expiry, every Interrupted Peer this Reactor itself dialled is given its re-dial attempt for this Frame (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.ProcessRedials()) — a schedule derived from the observed Pump interval just recorded above and the effective Linger, never a separate attempt-count knob, so a Peer whose Linger closed it this same Frame is never also given one. Throws InvalidOperationException if called from any thread other than the one that constructed this Reactor, or from inside a Pump already in progress. public void Pump()

ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.Send.title: Method Send | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.Send.summary: Method Send Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) Frames message as a u32 big-endian length prefix followed by its bytes (ReactorSockets.Session.MessageFramingCodec, ADR 0010) and appends the framed bytes to peer's retention region. Nothing is written to the socket here, ever (write batching) — a successful append only sets this Peer's pending-write marker (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot.HasPendingRetentionWrite), which the next Pump()'s explicit flush step (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.FlushPendingRetentionWrites()) drains in a single write carrying everything queued, including whatever was already sitting there. A Send with no following Pump call puts nothing on the wire. Refuses once a Goodbye has passed in either direction — this end's own (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot.LocalGoodbyeSent) or the far end's arrived and this Peer is already PeerClosing or on its way to PeerClosed (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot.PendingCloseReasonAfterRetentionDrains) — since a Message queued after a Goodbye is not one the far end has any business receiving. Also refuses a Peer whose handshake has not reached ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.HandshakeState.Established with NotEstablished: flushing that Message would write to a socket whose connect has not resolved, closing the Peer with TransportFailed, or send it before the far end's handshake record has been read. public SendOutcome Send(PeerId peer, ReadOnlySpan<byte> message) Parameters peer PeerId The Peer to send to. Throws if not open, matching CountersOf(PeerId). message ReadOnlySpan<byte> The Message payload, unframed. Throws if empty or longer than MaxMessageSize — the same bounds the receive side enforces, so this can never frame a Message the far end would reject. Returns SendOutcome Remarks ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot.IsInterrupted is deliberately not one of the refusal conditions above (ADR 0010's backpressure rule): a Send against an Interrupted Peer is exactly as welcome as one against a live Peer, because holding retention across the interruption for a possible Resume is the entire point of not closing the Peer in the first place. The append behaves identically either way — the difference is only downstream, in ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.FlushRetention(ReactorSockets.Core.SlotHandle, ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot)'s own IsInterrupted guard, which leaves these bytes queued rather than attempting a dead socket. Once the ring genuinely has no room, ReactorSockets.Core.RetentionOutcome.Exhausted reports the same way it would for a live Peer — the ring does not know or care why nothing has drained it — so an interruption that outlasts the send rate reaches RetentionExhausted exactly like a single oversized Message or a sustained rate would, the third of the three paths ADR 0010 names to it.

ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.html.summary: Class StreamSessionReactor Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll The stream Session profile (ADR 0010): Sessions established over TCP, addressed as Peers, delivering u32 length-prefixed Messages rather than the byte runs the transport gives. Construction validates StreamSessionOptions and its allocation bill and binds the declared endpoint set; each Peer is carried through the handshake to an established Session. Each established Peer reassembles Messages in its own persistent receive buffer and delivers each whole one as a MessageReceived event copied into the shared frame arena. public sealed class StreamSessionReactor : IDisposable Inheritance object StreamSessionReactor Implements IDisposable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks There is no cookie, no ack, no sequence space, no fragment and no RTO in this profile: TCP already provides what those were built for. The datagram Session protocol is deliberately not carried over TCP, because that would put retransmission on top of retransmission. Send timing (ADR 0011). Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) is off, unconditionally, on every stream Session socket — it is not a knob on StreamSessionOptions and cannot be turned back on. In its place, every Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) queued since the last Pump() is written to the wire together, once, by that Pump() call: batching we do ourselves, on our own schedule, rather than the connection's delayed acknowledgements deciding when a small Message may leave. That is a better version of what Nagle exists for, without Nagle's cost — a small Message waiting up to a round trip behind outstanding data — so a consumer measuring latency needs to know which of the two is doing the batching: theirs, by calling Pump() less often, or ours, always. Constructors StreamSessionReactor(StreamSessionOptions) Validates options — every knob and cross-check, then the frame arena's floor — before anything is allocated or bound, then binds every declared endpoint in the order supplied. A bind that fails throws here, naming the endpoint: binding is part of what this Reactor is, so there is no half-built Reactor to hand back. Properties BoundEndpoints The endpoints this Reactor is bound to right now, in the order they were declared. A snapshot: it answers what is bound, and there is no member that binds another — there is no rebinding (ADR 0014), and unlike the datagram profile a stream dial never binds a wildcard socket of its own, since TCP's own connect already binds an ephemeral local port implicitly. Counters A point-in-time snapshot of this Reactor's own counters (ADR 0013). No reset. Methods Close(PeerId) Announces this end is ending the Session with peer on purpose: attempts to append a Goodbye control record to whatever this Peer's retention region already holds, so it is the last thing flushed and everything queued before it is delivered first, then forbids any further Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) to it. If retention has no room for it yet, the attempt is retried on every later Pump (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.RetryGoodbyeAppends()) until it commits — Close(PeerId) must never leave the far end open indefinitely because the Goodbye it promised was silently dropped, and this end never closes itself locally until its own Goodbye has actually been appended and flushed. The PeerClosed carrying LocalClose is queued once that flush fully drains — immediately, on a later Pump, if nothing was queued when Close(PeerId) was called, or after however many Pumps a short write (or a retention append retry) takes to carry everything already retained plus the Goodbye itself. Idempotent: a stale PeerId, or a Peer already closing, is a no-op — a Peer closing under a caller, or a caller that closes the same Peer twice, is an ordinary race rather than a programmer error. Connect(IPEndPoint) Begins a Session with destination, returning the PeerId that will address it. The Peer occupies a capacity Slot from this moment, exactly as a dialling Link does in RawReactor: the handshake is work this Reactor is holding, and pretending otherwise would let a consumer dial past capacity and discover it only on the far side of a round trip. PeerConnected or PeerClosed resolves it on a later Pump. CountersOf(PeerId) A point-in-time snapshot of one Peer's counters (ADR 0013). Throws if the Peer is not open. Mirrors CountersOf(LinkId)'s shape for the Raw profile. Dispose() Releases every socket this Reactor bound or accepted. A Reactor owns every socket it bound, so a consumer that drops one without disposing it leaks those sockets until each Socket's finalizer runs. No PeerClosed events are queued: nothing can drain a disposed Reactor. Idempotent; every other member throws ObjectDisposedException afterwards. Drain() Drains every event produced this Frame — since the last Pump() — in the order it was produced. Pump() One synchronous advance: records this call's arrival against the last one (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.ObservedPumpInterval) before anything else, then wipes the previous Frame's events — which is also the moment a Peer still PeerClosing only because the last Frame's Messages had not been drained past yet becomes eligible to close (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.RetryPeersPendingClose()) — then admits ready connections, advances every in-flight dial and reads whatever bound socket is ready right now, running the handshake for everything that arrived. Every Peer whose received count advanced somewhere in that work — this Frame's own reads, or a held-back Message finally delivered by ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.RetryPeersWithBufferedMessages() — then has its delivery counter emitted exactly once (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.EmitDeliveryCounters()), before every Peer's queued retention bytes are flushed exactly once (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.FlushPendingRetentionWrites()) regardless of how many Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) calls queued them. Finally, every established Peer's two independent idle timers are enforced in one scan (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.EnforceIdleTimers()): a Peer from which nothing has been received for ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot.RemoteSendIdleInterval × ResolvedMissedHeartbeats moves to PeerInterrupted, an already-Interrupted Peer instead closes with LingerExpired once its effective Linger has elapsed since the interruption, and every surviving Peer that has written nothing to the wire — including whatever this Frame's own flush just carried — for at least SendIdleInterval sends the same delivery-counter record as a heartbeat, unconditionally and regardless of whether anything was ever received from it. Once idle timers may have closed an Interrupted Peer on Linger expiry, every Interrupted Peer this Reactor itself dialled is given its re-dial attempt for this Frame (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.ProcessRedials()) — a schedule derived from the observed Pump interval just recorded above and the effective Linger, never a separate attempt-count knob, so a Peer whose Linger closed it this same Frame is never also given one. Throws InvalidOperationException if called from any thread other than the one that constructed this Reactor, or from inside a Pump already in progress. Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) Frames message as a u32 big-endian length prefix followed by its bytes (ReactorSockets.Session.MessageFramingCodec, ADR 0010) and appends the framed bytes to peer's retention region. Nothing is written to the socket here, ever (write batching) — a successful append only sets this Peer's pending-write marker (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.PeerSlot.HasPendingRetentionWrite), which the next Pump()'s explicit flush step (ReactorSockets.StreamSessionReactor.FlushPendingRetentionWrites()) drains in a single write carrying everything queued, including whatever was already sitting there. A Send with no following Pump call puts nothing on the wire. ReactorSockets.html.summary: Namespace ReactorSockets Namespaces ReactorSockets.Logging Classes DatagramSessionOptions The construction surface of a DatagramSessionReactor (ADR 0012): the shared L0 budget composed in as Reactor, plus the knobs this profile alone has. Composed rather than inherited, so that nothing protocol-specific here can ever leak into ReactorOptions and turn it into the base class ADR 0011 refused. DatagramSessionReactor The datagram Session profile (ADR 0009): Sessions established over UDP, addressed as Peers, driven by a single synchronous Pump() from the consumer's own loop. It carries the handshake and everything that guards it — the stateless cookie, the amplification bound, version and capacity refusals, session identity and demultiplexing — and the data plane behind it: packet records in four sequence Spaces, one per DeliveryMode, fragmentation of reliable Messages, acknowledgement and retransmission, heartbeats, Goodbye, interruption and Resume. DiagnosticFormatter The one authoritative rendering of a DiagnosticRecord to text (ADR 0005, ADR 0013), so a structured Sink consumes the typed fields and never formats, and a text Sink gets this library's wording rather than inventing its own. Holds no state: nothing is allocated until Format(in DiagnosticRecord) is called, and a consumer who never formats pays nothing. RawReactor The escape hatch (ADR 0007): a consumer registers UDP sockets at runtime, gets a LinkId back for each, and advances everything with a single synchronous Pump() call from their own loop. Nothing is delivered except in response to a call the consumer made, on the thread that constructed this Reactor. TCP joins the datagram surface here: a listening Link and the connections it accepts are registered and admitted the same way, and a stream Link's reads drain as SegmentReceived and EndOfStream exactly like a datagram Link's. A stream Link's Send(LinkId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) takes what the socket will take and reports the count, arming exactly one Writable when it took fewer bytes than offered; Shutdown(LinkId) sends this Link's own FIN while it stays open for reading. ReactorOptions The budget L0 spends inside a Pump, shared by every profile. Composed as a member into each profile's options type rather than inherited from a base (ADR 0012) — nothing protocol-specific may ever enter this type, since a knob two of three profiles need is exactly what would turn it into the base class ADR 0011 refused. StreamSessionOptions The construction surface of a StreamSessionReactor (ADR 0011): the shared L0 budget composed in as Reactor, plus the knobs this profile alone has. Composed rather than inherited, so that nothing protocol-specific here can ever leak into ReactorOptions and turn it into the base class ADR 0011 refused. StreamSessionReactor The stream Session profile (ADR 0010): Sessions established over TCP, addressed as Peers, delivering u32 length-prefixed Messages rather than the byte runs the transport gives. Construction validates StreamSessionOptions and its allocation bill and binds the declared endpoint set; each Peer is carried through the handshake to an established Session. Each established Peer reassembles Messages in its own persistent receive buffer and delivers each whole one as a MessageReceived event copied into the shared frame arena. Structs DiagnosticRecord A single diagnostic emitted to an IReactorDiagnostics Sink: a closed DiagnosticId, its fixed DiagnosticLevel, a tagged subject — none, Link, Source or Peer (ADR 0013) — and two numeric slots whose meaning is documented per DiagnosticId member. No strings, no object[], no closures — everything here lives on the stack and is built only after IsEnabled(DiagnosticLevel) passes. LinkCounters A point-in-time snapshot of one Link's counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from that Link's registration, with no reset, fetched by value and keyed by LinkId — there is no accessor that enumerates every Link's counters in one call. LinkId A Link's identity: the Reactor that issued it, a zero-based slot index, and a generation counter that increments when the slot is reused, so a stale LinkId held past a Link's close compares unequal to whatever now occupies that slot (ADR 0014) rather than aliasing it. PeerCounters A point-in-time snapshot of one Peer's counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from that Peer's establishment, with no reset, fetched by value and keyed by PeerId — mirrors LinkCounters's Raw-profile shape and the same "no accessor enumerates every Peer's counters in one call" rule. PeerId A Peer's identity inside this process: the Reactor that issued it, a zero-based Slot index, and a generation counter that increments when the Slot is reused, so a stale PeerId held past a Peer's close compares unequal to whatever now occupies that Slot (ADR 0007) rather than aliasing it. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010), exactly as LinkId is the Raw profile's. RawEvent One event drained from a RawReactor. A ref struct because Payload aliases the frame arena directly and must never outlive the Frame it was drained in (ADR 0008). Kind determines exactly which other fields are populated — the kinds are DatagramReceived, Closed, Accepted, Connected, SegmentReceived, EndOfStream and Writable — the complete Raw profile roster. RawEventEnumerator The zero-allocation enumerator Drain() returns. A ref struct so that a foreach over it can yield RawEvent — itself a ref struct — without a heap-allocated IEnumerator<T>, following the same pattern as Span<T>'s own enumerator. ReactorCounters A point-in-time snapshot of the Reactor-scope counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from construction, with no reset. Fetched by value so nothing lets a consumer hold a pointer into live state across a Pump; diffing two snapshots gives everything a reset would, from state the consumer already owns. Result The outcome of an operation whose failures are the caller's to check rather than the runtime's to throw — a wrong-kind call on a Link (Send on a datagram Link) or a send the remote end or the network refused. Error names the illegality or the platform failure in prose; there is no error code enumeration here because, unlike CloseReason, nothing about this failure needs to survive as permanent public API — a consumer branches on IsSuccess and logs or surfaces Error as-is. SendResult The outcome of one Send(LinkId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) call. Unlike Result, a stream send has a quantity worth reporting even on success: the Reactor holds no outbound bytes (ADR 0008), so Send takes what the socket will take right now and hands back the count — the caller keeps whatever was not taken, and BytesSent is how it learns how much that is. SessionEvent One event drained from a Session Reactor. A ref struct because Payload aliases the frame arena directly, and must never outlive the Frame it was drained in (ADR 0008). Kind determines exactly which other fields are populated. SessionEventEnumerator The zero-allocation enumerator every Session Reactor's Drain returns (ADR 0010), shared by both profiles via ReactorSockets.ISessionEventSource rather than duplicated per profile. A ref struct so that a foreach over it can yield SessionEvent — itself a ref struct — without a heap-allocated IEnumerator<T>, following the same pattern as Span<T>'s own enumerator. Source Who a datagram claims to be from — an unauthenticated hint about origin, never an identity (ADR 0014). Carried on the record path as a value type: { family, 16 address bytes, scope id, port }, roughly 56 bytes, so a Diagnostic or an Event never allocates to name a Source. Interfaces IReactorDiagnostics The Diagnostic Sink contract. Implementations are called synchronously, on the consumer's thread, inside Pump — a Sink that stalls stalls the Frame, and a Sink that throws is caught, counted as SinkFaulted, and disabled for the life of the Reactor (ADR 0005). Calling back into the Reactor from a Sink is a programmer error and throws. Enums CloseReason Why a Link closed, defined and kept stable by this library rather than borrowed from a platform enumeration (ADR 0008): a consumer's permanent logic switches on this instead of a SocketError that differs between Windows and Unix. The exact SocketError travels in the DiagnosticRecord emitted at the same moment, linked to this only by the Link and the Pump it happened in. DeliveryMode Which of a datagram Session's four delivery modes carries a Message sent through Send(PeerId, DeliveryMode, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) (ADR 0009). See docs/delivery-modes.md for the consumer-facing guide to choosing one and the full guarantees each mode makes: ordering, duplicate suppression, and what a late arrival does. Each mode is carried in its own Space. DiagnosticId A closed, permanent enumeration of diagnostic causes with explicit values in reserved blocks — common 1-99, Raw 100-199, datagram session 200-299, stream session 300-399 (ADR 0013) — so a future insertion cannot silently renumber an id a consumer has persisted. There is no None or Unknown member and zero is never used: every DiagnosticRecord has a cause by construction. DiagnosticLevel The minimum severity a IReactorDiagnostics Sink was installed to receive. Ordered by ascending severity so that a level is enabled when it is at least as severe as the installed MinimumLevel. DiagnosticSubjectKind Which field of a DiagnosticRecord's tagged subject is populated (ADR 0013). A record has exactly one subject, so a Sink or formatter switches on this rather than checking several optional fields for which one is set. DisconnectReason Why a Peer's Session ended, defined and kept stable by this library rather than borrowed from a platform enumeration. Deliberately not shared with the Raw profile's CloseReason (ADR 0008): most of the members a Session needs are protocol vocabulary Raw can never produce, and a single shared enumeration would leave one profile documenting members it cannot emit. RawEventKind Which kind of RawEvent a drained event is (ADR 0008). Accepted comes from a listening Link, Connected from dialling, SegmentReceived and EndOfStream from stream reads, and Writable from partial sends. SendOutcome The outcome of one Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) call. A bare enum rather than a result struct (unlike SendResult): a Session-level send has no partial-completion quantity worth reporting back — the framed Message either fit in the Peer's retention region whole, or it did not, so the outcome is the whole story. SessionEventKind Which kind of SessionEvent was drained, and therefore which of its fields carry meaning. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010). SourceFamily The address family of a Source, carried as an explicit tag rather than inferred from the address bytes (ADR 0014). With DualMode never set, nothing in a 16-byte field distinguishes a zero-padded IPv4 address from an IPv6 one.
